schools.summary: Prefer the reading for liberty did Christ make us free on strong external evidence, take the case as dative of purpose, and hold that the verse belongs with the previous chapter.

Enumerate the liberty exactly and guard it at both ends: freedom from the law as covenant and curse but not from obedience to it as a rule; and refuse to reduce it to ceremonies, tracing it to the curse borne by Christ and defending liberty of conscience against ecclesiastical tyranny even to death.
Read the imperative as the weight of the verse: liberty is kept only by vigilance, since Satan attacks the Gospel wherever it appears, and the freedom in question is Christ’s and not any civil grant.
Take it as enfranchisement from the ceremonial yoke and the moral curse, owed wholly to Christ’s merit and royal authority, and therefore binding us to stand fast.
Read the liberty narrowly, as freedom from the ceremonial law.
Locate the rebuke in the word again: those who have felt the yoke and return to it are without excuse.

debates: Whether the received text or the variant for liberty did Christ make us free should be read.
Whether the liberty is exemption from ceremonies (Wesley, and the plain sense) or a whole deliverance from sin, Satan and death of which ceremonies are one department (Calvin).
How again can be said to Gentiles who had never been under the law — raised and answered only by Calvin.
outliers: Barnes alone holds the verse is misplaced by the chapter division and belongs to chapter four.
Calvin alone turns the verse into a defence of the Reformation against the charge of licentiousness.

2.pericope_label: Circumcision forfeits Christ; the circumcised man is debtor to the whole law

schools.summary: Weigh the grammar and the personal authority of the appeal, restrict the statement to circumcision sought as a ground of justification, and read the debt as a whole-system obligation assumed by the act — Christ a whole Saviour, or none.

Treat the verse as a touchstone for judging every doctrine, work and ceremony: anything added to faith in Christ as necessary to salvation falls under this sentence, and the law itself falling under it condemns human tradition the more.

Resolve the difficulty by distinguishing two aspects of circumcision in Paul — seal of the righteousness of faith in one place, bare legal covenant of merit here — and press the arithmetic of grace: dividing salvation between Christ and works forfeits Christ entirely.
Read the obligation plainly as an undertaking to fulfil every precept, and restrict the address to Gentiles.

debates: Whether the sentence is absolute or limited to circumcision sought as necessary to justification — Barnes and Calvin both limit it, Luther states it without qualification.
How Paul’s own circumcision of Timothy stands with it: Barnes pleads expediency, Calvin pleads a difference of aspect in the rite itself.
Whether every man means every man whatever (Gill, Barnes) or every Gentile (Wesley).
Whether again means a second testimony (Barnes’ own view) or simply furthermore (Bloomfield, reported by Barnes).
outliers: Wesley alone restricts every man to Gentiles.
Luther alone reads the debtor clause negatively as well as affirmatively, so that the circumcised man not only owes the whole law but in the very act of circumcision fails to keep any of it.

4.pericope_label: Fallen from grace; the hope of righteousness; faith working by love

schools.summary: Read the falling as a real apostasy in which grace already communicated to the soul is lost, with no assurance of recovery; and make operative love the touchstone by which every creed is tried, faith without it being dead.

Blunt the pastoral alarm by grammar and definition — a supposition (Barnes), a lost standing rather than a lost disposition (Ellicott), a change of sphere and not a lapse into occasional sin (Robertson) — and read the hoped-for righteousness as one only finally actualised at the end.

Locate the error in mixture rather than denial: the smallest part of justification credited to the law renounces Christ entirely. Circumcision is not called useless in itself, only abolished since Christ came, and the abolition does not touch the sacraments.
Note that hope carries both senses in Scripture, the thing hoped for and the affection of the hoper, so the clause bears a double reading.

debates: Whether falling from grace describes a real loss of salvation (Clarke), a merely supposed case (Barnes), a cancelled relation rather than a lost inward state (Ellicott), or a change of the sphere one stands in (Robertson).
Whether the righteousness hoped for is already possessed and awaiting confirmation (Ellicott’s ideal-then-actual scheme) or simply the justification received now by faith (Barnes, Wesley).
Whether the abolition of circumcision implies it was never of value — denied by Calvin, who dates the repeal to the revelation of Christ.
outliers: Clarke alone leaves the recovery of the fallen an open question.
Ellicott alone makes grace a divine act or relation rather than anything in the believer.
Clarke alone builds an argument on the etymology of the verb for waiting, and defends the derivation from Christian experience.

7.pericope_label: Ye did run well; who did hinder you; a little leaven; he that troubleth you

schools.summary: Work the vocabulary — the racecourse jostle, the broken-up road, the cut-in — and decline to identify the troubler, holding that the singular need not name a known man and that the judgment threatened is a trial rather than a sentence.

Read the leaven as corrupt doctrine rather than a faction, and Satan’s method as adulteration rather than open assault; note that Paul’s censure is framed to shame the Galatians back, and that the confidence he expresses points them to repentance as a gift of God.

Turn the passage on the afflicted conscience: the devil magnifies trifles into damnable crimes, and the cure is Paul’s own — that such a persuasion does not come from the God who called you. Defends trusting men as a fruit of charity without which common life would be impossible.
Grant that the rite is small in itself and press the consequence instead, that it obliges the whole law; place the blame on the Galatians’ own consent and on one chief troubler.
Draw the rule for discipline: distinguish always between those who spread error and those who follow it.

debates: What the hindering verb pictures: jostling on a racecourse (Doddridge, in Barnes), breaking up a road before an advancing army (Ellicott), or cutting in on a runner (Robertson).
Whether the little leaven is a little bad doctrine (Calvin) or a few seceders (Ellicott, Barnes, Wesley) — a flat contradiction between two of the strongest voices here.
Whether one identifiable ringleader is in view (Robertson on the singular, Wesley) or no particular person at all (Ellicott).
Whether shall bear his judgment means condemnation (Clarke) or being put on trial before God (Ellicott).
outliers: Robertson alone warns against reading the leaven as a symbol of evil rather than of pervasive power.
Luther alone raises, and answers, the question whether Paul may lawfully profess trust in men at all.

11.pericope_label: The offence of the cross; I would they were even cut off

schools.summary: Read the wish as a savage jest about self-mutilation, set against the local cult of Cybele, and admit both that Paul had once seemed to permit circumcision and that the language here falls short of Christ’s own gentleness — though Barnes rejects that reading as monstrous and takes the wish as excommunication.

Take the wish as exclusion from the church, defended lexically and explained by Paul’s weakened authority in Galatia; and distinguish conforming to the law out of condescension, which Paul allows, from teaching it as necessary, which he condemns absolutely.

Read it as a prayer for destruction, and justify the imprecation by subordinating the salvation of men to the glory of God; treat the persecution argument as an argument from the final cause and turn the charge of self-interest back on the false apostles.
Allow cursing when God’s word itself is blasphemed, and measure the gravity of the little leaven by the fact that Paul would curse for it.

debates: What cut off means: excommunication (Barnes, Clarke, Wesley), destruction by God’s hand (Gill, Calvin), or self-castration (Ellicott, Robertson, and the ancient Greek interpreters). Barnes reports the third reading only to call it monstrous.
Whether Paul had ever in fact given ground for the charge that he preached circumcision — Ellicott concedes he had, the rest treat it as pure slander built on the case of Timothy.
Whether an apostolic imprecation is defensible: Calvin and Luther both defend it on the ground of God’s glory and word, Ellicott declines to.
outliers: Ellicott alone criticises the Apostle, judging the verse short of the meekness and gentleness of Christ.
Barnes alone quotes the rival interpretation in Latin rather than English, and records his amazement that a lexicon had adopted it.
Calvin, defending the imprecation, states in passing that Christ suffered for the sins of the whole world and that God wills the salvation of all men without exception.
Wakefield’s conjecture that the verb means may lament it is reported by Clarke and rejected by him.

13.pericope_label: Liberty is not an occasion to the flesh; the whole law fulfilled in one word

schools.summary: Separate liberty itself, which lies in the conscience before God, from the use of it, which lies in outward dealings with men; and face squarely the difficulty that the whole law is said to be summed in the second table, answering that love of neighbour is the visible proof of an invisible piety.

Fix the boundary at the two laws — freedom from the ceremonial, tighter obligation under the moral, and Antinomianism as the name for confusing them — and read the summary commandment as implying love to God.

Repair the English (there is no word for use), locate the stress on serve, widen neighbour beyond the Israelite sense the original command had, and note the paradox of Paul enforcing the law he has been arguing against.
Hold that redemption from the law’s curse leaves its obligation untouched.
Treat the precept as the true superstructure on the foundation of Christ’s righteousness, and use it to rank works of charity far above ceremonies.

debates: How the whole law can be summed in the second table: Calvin rejects the answer that the first table is itself only love, and appeals instead to the visibility of neighbour-love; Gill and Wesley give the answer Calvin rejects.
Whether neighbour carries its original Israelite restriction or the wider sense Christ gave it (Ellicott, Robertson).
Whether the warning against fleshly licence reflects a real danger in Galatia or a caution imported from Corinth (Ellicott’s conjecture).
outliers: Clarke alone names the error — Antinomianism — and alone reports the variant reading in the love of the Spirit.
Robertson alone calls the appeal to the law a paradox and feels its force against Paul’s own argument.

15.pericope_label: Bite and devour one another; walk in the Spirit; the flesh against the Spirit

schools.summary: Correct the English (cannot do overtranslates; ye shall not is really a future), insist the Spirit meant is the Holy Spirit, deny that the flesh-Spirit antithesis is dualism about matter, and make flesh and law correlative so that release from one is release from the other.

Take flesh as the whole nature of man rather than the lower appetites, hear the exhortation as an accusation that the Galatians are carnal, trace the false doctrine itself to a judgment on their pride, and turn freedom from law into the acceptance of imperfect obedience.

Read the passage as a call to recover a Spirit actually grieved and lost, and take the frustrated desires to be those of the flesh, thwarted by the Spirit’s strength — with the corollary that Paul cannot be describing mature Christians.
Use the verse against the scholastic inference from love fulfils the law to the law justifies, and read church history as proof that once the foundation is overthrown, sects multiply without end.
Concede the continuing stirrings of corrupt nature while denying it dominion over those led by the Spirit.

debates: Whether ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh is a promise (Barnes, Robertson) or an imperative (the margin and Tindale, reported by Barnes).
What the will fails to accomplish in v17: the good it desires (Ellicott, Henry, and the Authorised rendering) or the evil the flesh desires (Wesley) — the two readings invert the verse.
Whether cannot do is a defensible translation at all — denied by Barnes on the strength of the Greek.
Whether the passage describes mature believers (Henry, Calvin) or the fallen state of these particular churches (Clarke).
Whether the verb for lusting may be predicated of the Spirit — Lightfoot says no, Robertson says the objection is needless.
outliers: Calvin alone treats the false doctrine as itself a chastisement sent from heaven for pride.
Ellicott alone raises and rejects the dualist reading of flesh and spirit.
Gill alone notes that Paul withholds the expected image of wolves entering the flock and makes the sheep the predators.

schools.summary: Classify the list, record the manuscript doubts over adultery and murders and the errors of the Authorised rendering, derive the sorcery word from pharmacy, decline to affirm that witchcraft was ever real, and rest the exclusion from the kingdom on the verb for habitual practice.

Insist that the sorcery named is literal witchcraft and that denying its reality denies the authority of both Testaments; observe that the works are plural and the fruit singular; and read the catalogue as chosen for these particular readers.
Answer the objection that the threat would exclude everyone by distinguishing sin from impenitence, and turn the passage against teachers who exchanged such instruction for disputes about ceremonies.
Read the parallel warning through its tense — such were some of you — so that the gravest of these sins is no bar to hope, and only persistent wickedness is condemned.
Direct the threat at those who boast of Gospel and Spirit while securely practising the flesh, on the chance that terror may start the fight.

debates: Whether witchcraft in this list is real sorcery (Wesley, emphatically) or a human imposture whose existence the apostle does not vouch for (Barnes) — with Clarke and Ellicott occupying the ground between.
How the catalogue divides: Ellicott and Robertson both find four groups but not the same four.
Whether adultery and murders belong in the text at all.
Whether the exclusion from the kingdom falls on the act or on the habit — resolved the same way by Calvin, Robertson and Cyril from three different starting points.
outliers: Wesley alone argues that the plural works and the singular fruit are theologically deliberate.
Clarke alone conjectures that murders entered the text by similarity of sound to the word before it.
Clarke alone illustrates misdirected zeal from the inquisitions.
Ellicott alone passes on the theory that all sin reduces to two instincts.

22.pericope_label: The fruit of the Spirit; against such there is no law

schools.summary: Read the change from works to fruit as deliberate and the graces as not traceable to the renewed heart itself; rank the list above the Stoic cardinal virtues; reclaim temperance from its narrow modern sense; and correct against such to mean such things, not such men — though Ellicott denies the works/fruit distinction has any substance.

Grant the pagan virtues their civil lustre and deny them any purity in God’s sight, and read no law as the withdrawal of the law’s dominion rather than its mere non-application, the law still teaching while the Spirit of adoption removes our subjection.

Take fruit as the more honourable name, hold that love alone would have sufficed since it extends to all the rest, and explain the freedom from law by the righteous man doing unconstrained what the law requires.
Call love the root of all the rest, define the graces closely, record the manuscripts that add chastity, and read the last clause as simple immunity from condemnation.
Turn the list into prayer, asking that the Spirit be sent so that these fruits may be rendered up.

debates: Whether fruit is deliberately opposed to works — pressed by Barnes, Robertson, Luther, Gill and Calvin, denied outright by Ellicott.
Whether peace here is reconciliation with God (Barnes) or peaceableness towards men (Ellicott’s preference from the context).

What against such there is no law asserts: that such lives escape condemnation (Clarke), that such things lie outside and above the sphere of law (Ellicott), or that where the Spirit reigns the law has lost its dominion though not its teaching office (Calvin, Luther).
Whether such is neuter or masculine — Ellicott corrects the older commentators.
outliers: Ellicott alone rejects the works/fruit distinction that the rest of the chapter’s commentary is built on.
Calvin alone names four Roman worthies in order to deny their virtues any standing before God.
Robertson alone scores Paul’s list against the Stoic canon virtue by virtue.

24.pericope_label: They that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh; live and walk in the Spirit; vainglory

schools.summary: Explain crucified from the believer’s union with a crucified Master and date it to baptism; read the aorist as a completed extermination; allow that the quickened life still needs human co-operation; and hear the closing warning as aimed at a known national temperament.

Assign the mortification to the cross rather than to the man, deny that the flesh is yet destroyed while denying it dominion, argue from soul and body that an indwelling Spirit must show outward effects, and trace provoking and envying alike to ambition.

Draw from the verse that God designs to save believers from all sin, inward and outward, while picturing the flesh as bound and growing continually weaker; decline to speculate about what occasioned the final warning.

Concede that the saints still feel anger, envy and impatience without accomplishing them, trace vainglory to pride as the head-spring of all sin, and distinguish praise of the man, which is a lie, from praise of the ministry, which is to be sought.

debates: How complete the crucifixion of the flesh already is: dead and powerless (Barnes, Ellicott), destined to be wholly destroyed in the believer (Clarke), not yet destroyed but dethroned (Calvin), still active though never consented to (Luther), or progressively weakened (Wesley).
Whether if we live in the Spirit means deriving life from him or living unto him (Ellicott gives both).
What occasioned the warning against vainglory — the Judaising teachers’ campaign against Paul, some internal matter, or nothing recoverable (Clarke).
outliers: Ellicott alone fixes the crucifixion of the flesh at the moment of baptism, and alone reports the older reading they that are of Christ Jesus.
Luther alone separates praise of the minister from praise of the ministry and makes the second a duty.
Gill alone stops to exclude the elect not yet called from the description.
